blocks.content: Arunachal Pradesh, the 'Land of the Rising Sun', has a rich and layered history that spans ancient civilisations, medieval kingdoms, colonial encounters, and modern statehood. Its historical evolution is a fascinating blend of indigenous tribal heritage and external political dynamics.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Arunachal Pradesh's history spans pre-historic, ancient, medieval, and colonial eras.
The British Colonial Period lasted from 1826 to 1947, shaping early administrative boundaries.
The McMahon Line represents a vital geopolitical boundary established during British rule.
The 1962 Sino-Indian War was a major historical turning point impacting post-independence governance.
Post-independence administrative evolution ultimately led to full statehood for Arunachal Pradesh.

blocks.content: Archaeological evidence suggests that Arunachal Pradesh has been inhabited since prehistoric times. Stone tools, megaliths, and cave paintings discovered at various sites indicate the presence of early human settlements. The region finds mention in ancient Indian texts such as the Kalika Purana and the Mahabharata, where it is referred to as the land of Kirata tribes.

items: The Idu Mishmis, Adis, and Nishis are considered among the oldest indigenous peoples of the region.
References to the region as 'Prabhu Mountains' and 'Lohit Valley' appear in ancient scriptures.
Megalithic structures (menhirs and monoliths) found across the region date back to approximately 2000 BCE.
The region was part of the ancient Kamarupa kingdom, which at its height covered much of Northeast India.
Excavations at Itanagar's Ita Fort region have yielded artefacts suggesting medieval settlement dating to the 14th–15th centuries CE.

blocks.content: During the medieval period, the region came under the influence of the Ahom kingdom of Assam and various local chieftainships. However, the dense forests and mountainous terrain largely insulated the tribes from direct conquest.

cells: Ahom kingdom expands towards foothills of present-day Arunachal
Construction of Ita Fort near Itanagar (Itakhola dynasty)
Chutia and Koch kingdoms exercise influence in lower foothills
Moamoria rebellion weakens Ahom hold; tribal autonomy increases

blocks.content: The Ita Fort, located near modern Itanagar, is one of the most significant medieval structures in the state. It is believed to have been built during the 14th–15th century and consists of brick structures spread over a large area. The name 'Itanagar' itself is derived from 'Ita', meaning brick in the local language.

The region's formal contact with British India began after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826), which ended the First Anglo-Burmese War and brought Assam under British control. The territories now forming Arunachal Pradesh were classified as 'excluded areas' or 'partially excluded areas' by the British, meaning they were not directly administered under ordinary provincial law.

items: 1838: First British political officer appointed for the region.
1873: The Inner Line Regulation was promulgated, creating a boundary between the hills and the plains. This required special permits for entry.
1914: The Simla Convention between British India, China, and Tibet established the McMahon Line as the boundary between British India and Tibet. China never ratified this agreement.
1912: The area was declared the North-East Frontier Tract (NEFT) under the administrative control of the Governor-General.
1919-1945: Several British expeditions were conducted to survey and establish administrative posts in the interior.
1944: During World War II, the region gained strategic importance as Japanese forces advanced through Myanmar and threatened Northeast India.

blocks.content: The McMahon Line is the de facto boundary between India and China in the eastern sector. It was drawn by Sir Henry McMahon during the Simla Convention of 1914. The line runs along the crest of the Himalayas and places approximately 90,000 square kilometres of territory within India, which forms present-day Arunachal Pradesh. China has historically disputed this line, claiming it was an imposition of colonial powers.

After India's independence in 1947, the region was reorganised and administered as the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA). This administrative structure was established to bring governance to the tribal areas while preserving their distinct cultural identity.

cells: India's Independence; region continues as NEFT under Assam Governor
Renamed North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA); capital at Shillong
Sino-Indian War; China occupies much of NEFA before withdrawing
NEFA renamed Arunachal Pradesh; becomes a Union Territory; capital shifts to Itanagar
Arunachal Pradesh gets elected Legislative Assembly for first time
Arunachal Pradesh attains full statehood on 20th February; becomes the 24th state of India
State celebrates 12 years of statehood; major developmental push begins

blocks.content: The 1962 Sino-Indian War and Its Impact

items: Duration of the British Colonial Period in the region (1826–1947).
Historical treaty, agreement, and significance associated with the McMahon Line.
Key political and territorial consequences of the 1962 Sino-Indian War.
Constitutional milestones leading from NEFA/Union Territory status to full Statehood.

blocks.content: The 1962 Sino-Indian War had a profound and lasting impact on Arunachal Pradesh. Chinese forces advanced rapidly across the McMahon Line in October 1962, capturing most of NEFA. However, China declared a unilateral ceasefire and withdrew to pre-war positions in November 1962. This conflict highlighted the strategic importance of the region and led to accelerated development of infrastructure, roads, and administrative machinery in subsequent years.

Arunachal Pradesh became a Union Territory on 20 January 1972 and was renamed from NEFA to Arunachal Pradesh on the same date. It achieved full statehood on 20 February 1987, becoming the 24th state of the Indian Union. The first Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh as a full state was Gegong Apang.

items: P.K. Thungan was the first Chief Minister when it became a Union Territory in 1975.
Prem Khandu Thungan (P.K. Thungan) served as the first Chief Minister of the Union Territory.
Gegong Apang was the longest-serving Chief Minister and led the state through much of its early statehood.
Dorjee Khandu was Chief Minister before his tragic death in a helicopter crash in April 2011.
Pema Khandu, son of Dorjee Khandu, became Chief Minister in 2016 and has continued to serve.
